# A projective boundary weight realized by an actual convex gauge erosion

This note independently verifies the proposed ordinary boundary weight
and supplies its direct geometric realization. It concerns one genuine
convex fiber. It does not projectively transform the mixed family or its
lattice, and it does not assert that independently eroding its fibers
preserves their anchored inclusions.

## 1. The single weight pays every through-source cap

Let K be a convex body in R^d, d>=1, with0 in its interior. Write
g_K for its Minkowski gauge, rho(u)>0 for its radial function on the unit
sphere, and h_K for its support function. At almost every boundary point
x, let n_K(x) be the outward unit normal. For d=1 the boundary measure
is counting measure and the two outward normals are used.

The ordinary boundary theorem in
`candidate 2d9458b5433d0a83`, using the attained
normalization from `candidate 85d2c2a949b59b29`, supplies
a vector a such that1+a dot x>0 on K and

    T_a(x)=x/(1+a dot x)

maps K to a convex body with centroid0. This note's independent radial
verification of its boundary identity is included to connect that weight
directly to the actual deformation below. The parent source owns the
full normalization and ordinary boundary-potential theorem.

Put delta=min_K(1+a dot x)>0 and define on the whole real line

    f(t)=t^(-d),                         t>=delta,
    f(t)=delta^(-d)-d delta^(-d-1)(t-delta), t<=delta. (1)

The derivatives agree at delta and are nondecreasing. Consequently f is
finite, positive, C1 and convex on R. For each unit normal n, the function

    Phi(n,x)=h_K(n) f(1+a dot x)                       (2)

is finite, nonnegative and convex in x on ALL R^d; h_K(n)>0 because0 is
interior. On the actual boundary it has the exact cap identity

    integral_(boundary K intersect H) Phi(n_K(x),x) dH_(d-1)(x)
        =d |T_a(K) intersect H|                       (3)

for every closed halfspace H through0. Indeed the projective map
preserves each ray and changes its radial length to
rho(u)/(1+a dot rho(u)u). Radial integration and the boundary cone
identity give both sides as

    integral_(sphere intersect H)
       rho(u)^d (1+a dot rho(u)u)^(-d) dH_(d-1)(u).

For completeness, the boundary cone identity is
integral_boundary (x dot n_K(x))psi(x)dH_(d-1)
=integral_sphere rho(u)^d psi(rho(u)u)dH_(d-1)(u).
It follows from the area formula for the Lipschitz radial parametrization,
whose surface Jacobian satisfies (n_K dot u)dS=rho^(d-1)du. Such a
parametrization is Lipschitz because K has both a positive inradius and
a finite outer radius. It is therefore valid without smoothness or strict
convexity. On the boundary x dot n_K(x)=h_K(n_K(x)). For d=1 the same
identity is the direct sum over the two rays.

Applying ordinary Grunbaum to the actual centroid-zero body T_a(K) yields

    integral_(boundary K intersect H) Phi dH_(d-1)
       >=Gamma_d integral_boundary K Phi dH_(d-1).     (4)

The SAME weight works simultaneously for every through0 cap. No comparison
between the original unweighted cap volume and its projective image is
claimed. A central cutting plane has zero weighted boundary mass: its
radial directions have sphere measure zero in d>=2, and in d=1 it misses
the two boundary points. Thus closed caps cause no boundary-mass omission.

## 2. Direct convex realization and uniform cap loss

For epsilon>=0 set

    K_epsilon={x:g_K(x)+epsilon f(1+a dot x)<=1}.         (5)

For all sufficiently small positive epsilon this is a convex body with
0 in its interior, contained in K. Convexity follows by adding two convex
functions; boundedness follows from g_K(x)>=|x|/R for an outer radius R.
At0 the defining value is epsilon f(1)<1. The bodies are nested as epsilon
increases because f>0. Hence this is an actual inward deformation, not
an arbitrary prescribed surface speed.

The exact radial endpoint r_epsilon(u) solves

    r_epsilon(u)/rho(u)
       +epsilon f(1+a dot r_epsilon(u)u)=1.             (6)

Choose epsilon small enough that the derivative in r of the left side
is uniformly positive on0<=r<=rho(u); this is possible because1/rho>=1/R
and f' is bounded on the compact range attained there. Equation(6) then
has its unique endpoint between0 and rho(u). It first gives
|r_epsilon-rho|<=C epsilon uniformly. Applying the Lipschitz bound for f
again gives the uniform expansion

    r_epsilon(u)=rho(u)
       -epsilon rho(u)f(1+a dot rho(u)u)+O(epsilon^2).  (7)

All constants depend on this fixed K and a, not on u or on a cap direction.
Integrating the dth radial powers over any sphere halfspace therefore gives

    |K intersect H|-|K_epsilon intersect H|
       =epsilon d|T_a(K) intersect H|+O(epsilon^2),     (8)

uniformly over ALL closed H through0. The total loss is

    |K|-|K_epsilon|=epsilon D+O(epsilon^2),
    D=d|T_a(K)|>0.                                    (9)

Equations(4),(8) show that every own-source cap loses at least
epsilon Gamma_d D-O(epsilon^2). For a halfspace containing0 whose boundary
does not pass through0, its parallel through0 halfspace is contained in it.
Nestedness therefore gives the same lower bound on removed mass there.

In the usual boundary language the first normal loss speed in(5) is
h_K(n_K(x)) f(1+a dot x)=Phi(n_K(x),x) at almost every boundary point.
The radial proof above proves its integrated first variation without
requiring a smooth boundary or a globally differentiable gauge.

## 3. A precise conditional multi-witness consequence

Suppose a mixed family has m DISTINCT assigned source fibers, with one
chosen interior source in each. Assume these fibers can be changed
simultaneously by sufficiently small prescribed inward Hausdorff
perturbations while preserving their exact anchored inclusions. For each
source construct(5), translating its source to0 first, and use parameter
epsilon/D_i so that every source has total loss derivative1.

Assume further that a fixed finite family of closed ambient caps through
each assigned source covers its assigned deepest base planes, and every
one of those caps has original mass at most Q=beta M. Suppose all other
base planes have finite fixed covers whose cap masses are at most Q-eta
for some eta>0. These are actual fixed covers, not moving cap thresholds.

Every assigned cap loses at least epsilon Gamma_d-O(epsilon^2) from its
own source fiber by(8). If its continuous normal is zero, its trace in
that fiber is the whole fiber and the loss is instead epsilon+O(epsilon^2),
which is at least as strong. All additional erosion losses are nonnegative.
The original closed caps still cover exactly the same base planes; their
assigned raw mass bounds are therefore at most

    Q-epsilon Gamma_d+O(epsilon^2).

The old slack-cover masses can only decrease by nesting, so remain below
this bound for small epsilon. The actual new global maximum normalized
depth is consequently at most

    [Q-epsilon Gamma_d+O(epsilon^2)]/[M-m epsilon+O(epsilon^2)]
      =beta+epsilon(m beta-Gamma_d)/M+O(epsilon^2).     (10)

If beta<Gamma_d/m this is a strict decrease. NO regularity of the fixed
caps, proper-coarea formula, response equalization, or supporting-face
allocation is needed. Positive mass on an ambient cap boundary is retained
by the closed-cap inclusion and nesting argument. The assigned source
remains interior to its new fiber for all sufficiently small epsilon.

A sufficient explicit freedom condition is that every extreme anchored
Minkowski inclusion affected by at least one chosen fiber has STRICT
compact containment in its target. Indeed there are finitely many such
extreme representations. Let delta>0 be their smallest support margin.
If all changed fibers have Hausdorff displacement less than delta/3,
the target support changes by less than delta/3 and the weighted input
support sum by less than delta/3, since its coefficients sum to one.
Thus each affected inclusion remains valid; unaffected inclusions are
unchanged. All representations follow from the extreme ones by linearity
of support functions. The convex hull therefore retains exactly the
prescribed fibers on the complete base. This argument permits simultaneous
changes on both sides of an anchored inclusion and does not mistakenly
use the one-fiber input-or-target dichotomy.

If the integer base spans R^n, this hull is itself an ambient convex body.
For a lower-rank complete integer base, its affine hull is rational; the
orthogonal projection of the integer lattice onto its direction-space
complement is a discrete lattice. Relative to any one of its integer
points, nonzero projected integer offsets thus have a positive minimum
norm. Taking a sufficiently small fixed ball in that complementary
integer subspace gives a full ambient convex body without adding any
integer base or changing any prescribed fiber. This supplies the same
actual realization if ambient nonempty interior is required.

This corollary does not infer m<=2^n, simultaneous fiber freedom,
interior sources, or the required finite covers for an
arbitrary mixed body. In particular it does not bypass active anchored
contacts. Its concrete new input is the same-source cap payment for
arbitrary fiber shapes and arbitrary through-source normals.
